suite.name: Diet Durability (Low-Carb vs Low-Fat)
suite.query: Do randomized controlled trials show that low-carbohydrate diets produce greater weight loss than low-fat diets, and does the difference persist over time?
suite.focus: Multi-arm attribution, short vs long-term persistence, null findings

executive_summary.bottom_line: Empirical findings show divergence depending on specific study conditions, protocols, and outcome measures.
executive_summary.overall_evidence_assessment: suggests context-dependent effects or qualified disagreement
executive_summary.strongest_supporting_evidence: Effects of low-carbohydrate diets versus low-fat diets on metabolic risk factors in overweight and obese adults: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials: Compared with participants on LFD, participants on LCD had a greater reduction in triglycerides (-0.14 mmol/L; 95% CI, -0.18 to -0.10 mmol/L), diastolic blood pressure (-0.87 mmHg; 95% CI, -1.41 to -0.32 mmHg), weight loss (-1.33 kg; 95% CI, -1.79 to -0.87 kg), and a greater increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (0.07 mmol/L; 95% CI, 0.06 to 0.09 mmol/L) in 6-23 months.
executive_summary.strongest_conflicting_evidence: Long-term Effects of a Very Low-Carbohydrate Diet and a Low-Fat Diet on Mood and Cognitive Function: RESULTS: By 1 year, the overall mean (SE) weight loss was 13.7 (1.8) kg, with no significant difference between groups (P = .26).
executive_summary.why_studies_disagree: Differences in measurement protocols, baseline conditions, exposure degrees, and study settings.

subclaim_assessments.subclaim: Trial weight-loss comparison: Randomized controlled trials show low-carbohydrate diets produce greater weight loss than low-fat diets in short-term horizons.
subclaim_assessments.rationale: Directly addressed by empirical evidence claims in papers: W4292401731.

subclaim_assessments.subclaim: Long-term persistence: The difference in weight loss between low-carbohydrate and low-fat diets persists over time.
subclaim_assessments.rationale: Qualified: trials show initial weight loss differences attenuate over time and are no longer statistically significant at 12 months.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Effects of low-carbohydrate diets versus low-fat diets on metabolic risk factors in overweight and obese adults: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Compared with participants on LFD, participants on LCD had a greater reduction in triglycerides (-0.14 mmol/L; 95% CI, -0.18 to -0.10 mmol/L), diastolic blood pressure (-0.87 mmHg; 95% CI, -1.41 to -0.32 mmHg), weight loss (-1.33 kg; 95% CI, -1.79 to -0.87 kg), and a greater increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (0.07 mmol/L; 95% CI, 0.06 to 0.09 mmol/L) in 6-23 months.
evidence_ledger.outcome: Reduction in triglycerides, diastolic blood pressure, and weight; increase in HDL cholesterol
evidence_ledger.population_setting: Participants on LFD or LCD diets

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Effects of low-carbohydrate diets versus low-fat diets on metabolic risk factors in overweight and obese adults: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: However, the decrease of total cholesterol (0.14 mmol/L; 95% CI, 0.07 to 0.20 mmol/L) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (0.10 mmol/L; 95% CI, 0.06 to 0.14 mmol/L) was more conducive to LFD in 6-23 months.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Effects of low-carbohydrate diets versus low-fat diets on metabolic risk factors in overweight and obese adults: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: The meta-analysis compared the effects of LCD (carbohydrate intake ≤ 40%) with LFD (fat intake < 30%) on metabolic risk factors and weight loss for ≥6 months.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Comparing the Efficacy and Safety of Low-Carbohydrate Diets with Low-Fat Diets for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Compared with LFDs, treatment with LCDs achieved significant reduced HbA1c by 0.35% (95% CI: −0.45, −0.24; P < 0.00001).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Comparing the Efficacy and Safety of Low-Carbohydrate Diets with Low-Fat Diets for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: LCDs appeared to be more beneficial in decreasing body weight than LFDs (WMD = −2.99 kg; 95% CI: −4.36, −1.63; P < 0.0001), especially in the subgroup that used VLCDs (WMD = −9.49 kg; 95% CI: −12.88, −6.09, P < 0.00001).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Comparing the Efficacy and Safety of Low-Carbohydrate Diets with Low-Fat Diets for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: For cardiovascular risk factors, the LCD interventions significantly reduced TG concentration (WMD: −0.20 mmol/l; 95% CI: −0.31, −0.10; P = 0.0001) and increased HDL-C concentration (WMD: 0.09 mmol/l; 95% CI: 0.05,0.13; P < 0.00001).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Effects of a low carbohydrate diet on energy expenditure during weight loss maintenance: randomized trial
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: RESULTS: Total energy expenditure differed by diet in the intention-to-treat analysis (n=162, P=0.002), with a linear trend of 52 kcal/d (95% confidence interval 23 to 82) for every 10% decrease in the contribution of carbohydrate to total energy intake (1 kcal=4.18 kJ=0.00418 MJ).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Effects of a low carbohydrate diet on energy expenditure during weight loss maintenance: randomized trial
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: In the per protocol analysis (n=120, P<0.001), the respective differences were 131 kcal/d (-6 to 267) and 278 kcal/d (144 to 411).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Effects of a low carbohydrate diet on energy expenditure during weight loss maintenance: randomized trial
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Among participants in the highest third of pre-weight loss insulin secretion, the difference between the low and high carbohydrate diet was 308 kcal/d in the intention-to-treat analysis and 478 kcal/d in the per protocol analysis (P<0.004).

suite.name: Alcohol & Mortality Confounding
suite.query: Does moderate alcohol consumption reduce all-cause mortality, or can the apparent protective association be explained by study design and confounding?
suite.focus: Observational vs trial classification, association vs causation, confounding

executive_summary.bottom_line: Empirical findings show divergence depending on specific study conditions, protocols, and outcome measures.
executive_summary.overall_evidence_assessment: suggests context-dependent effects or qualified disagreement
executive_summary.strongest_supporting_evidence: Do “Moderate” Drinkers Have Reduced Mortality Risk? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Alcohol Consumption and All-Cause Mortality: RESULTS: Without adjustment, meta-analysis of all 87 included studies replicated the classic J-shaped curve, with low-volume drinkers (1.3-24.9 g ethanol per day) having reduced mortality risk (RR = 0.86, 95% CI [0.83, 0.90]).
executive_summary.strongest_conflicting_evidence: No conflicting studies found in sampled literature.
executive_summary.why_studies_disagree: Differences in measurement protocols, baseline conditions, exposure degrees, and study settings.
executive_summary.confidence_and_limitations: Evidence synthesis is based on retrieved open-access scholarly literature. Heuristic comparison scores reflect condition similarity, not formal statistical meta-analysis.
executive_summary.research_coverage: Retrieved 10 candidate papers; examined 8 in depth (1 open-access full texts).

subclaim_assessments.subclaim: Mortality reduction: Moderate alcohol consumption causally reduces all-cause mortality.
subclaim_assessments.rationale: Qualified: observational studies observe an inverse association (J-shaped curve) between moderate alcohol intake and all-cause mortality, but causality is not established by randomized trials, and the apparent protective association is largely attenuated after controlling for abstainer reference-group misclassification (sick-quitters) and residual socioeconomic confounding.

subclaim_assessments.subclaim: Confounding and bias: The apparent protective association can be explained by study design limitations, reference-group definitions, and confounding.
subclaim_assessments.rationale: Supported: methodological analyses and systematic evaluations indicate apparent protective mortality associations are substantially driven by reference-group misclassification (e.g., former drinkers / sick-quitters) and residual confounding.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Do “Moderate” Drinkers Have Reduced Mortality Risk? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Alcohol Consumption and All-Cause Mortality
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: RESULTS: Without adjustment, meta-analysis of all 87 included studies replicated the classic J-shaped curve, with low-volume drinkers (1.3-24.9 g ethanol per day) having reduced mortality risk (RR = 0.86, 95% CI [0.83, 0.90]).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Do “Moderate” Drinkers Have Reduced Mortality Risk? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Alcohol Consumption and All-Cause Mortality
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Occasional drinkers (<1.3 g per day) had similar mortality risk (RR = 0.84, 95% CI [0.79, 0.89]), and former drinkers had elevated risk (RR = 1.22, 95% CI [1.14, 1.31]).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Do “Moderate” Drinkers Have Reduced Mortality Risk? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Alcohol Consumption and All-Cause Mortality
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: After adjustment for abstainer biases and quality-related study characteristics, no significant reduction in mortality risk was observed for low-volume drinkers (RR = 0.97, 95% CI [0.88, 1.07]).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: All cause mortality and the case for age specific alcohol consumption guidelines: pooled analyses of up to 10 population based cohorts
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Among younger men, the range of protective effects was minimal, with a significant reduction in hazards present only among those who reported consuming 15.1-20.0 units/average week (hazard ratio 0.49, 95% confidence interval 0.26 to 0.91) or 0.1-1.5 units on the heaviest day (0.43, 0.21 to 0.87).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: All cause mortality and the case for age specific alcohol consumption guidelines: pooled analyses of up to 10 population based cohorts
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Supplementary analyses found that most protective effects disappeared where calculated in comparison with various definitions of occasional drinkers.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Moderate alcohol consumption and cardiovascular risk reduction: open issues
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: This will be based on findings from theliterature, with a particular emphasis on meta-analyses.Results and Conclusion: The role of different alcoholic beverages, age and sex, confounding, former drinkersand study design has been discussed.Whether wine is better than beer or spirits, though suggestive, remains to be established.Cardiovascular morbidity and total mortality is significantly reduced both in men and women who are regulardrinkers of low amounts of alcohol; however, the predicted protection in women disappears at lower dosesthan in men.The primary protection of alcohol decreases after adjustment for known variables, thus confirming the importanceof confounding in assessing drinking effects, but it remains significant and of undoubted public health value.As the cardiovascular protection by moderate alcohol consumption might have been unduly overestimated byinclusion in control groups of former drinkers, we compared studies that used as a reference group the categoryof no alcohol intake and/or formally excluded former drinkers with studies which did not: the protection wasindeed somewhat lower in the former than in the latter studies, but was still statistically significant.We conclude that the dose-response relationship between alcohol intake and cardiovascular risk or totalmortality, consistently described by J-shaped curves, can be reasonably attributed to a combination of bothreal beneficial (at lower doses) and harmful (at higher doses) effects of alcohol or wine consumption.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Mortality in England and Wales attributable to current alcohol consumption
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: RESULTS: Because of the cardioprotective properties of alcohol, it is estimated that there are approximately 2% fewer deaths annually in England and Wales than would be expected in a non-drinking population.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Association of alcohol consumption with selected cardiovascular disease outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: RESULTS: The pooled adjusted relative risks for alcohol drinkers relative to non-drinkers in random effects models for the outcomes of interest were 0.75 (95% confidence interval 0.70 to 0.80) for cardiovascular disease mortality (21 studies), 0.71 (0.66 to 0.77) for incident coronary heart disease (29 studies), 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81) for coronary heart disease mortality (31 studies), 0.98 (0.91 to 1.06) for incident stroke (17 studies), and 1.06 (0.91 to 1.23) for stroke mortality (10 studies).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Association of alcohol consumption with selected cardiovascular disease outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Secondary analysis of mortality from all causes showed lower risk for drinkers compared with non-drinkers (relative risk 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92)).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Association of alcohol consumption with selected cardiovascular disease outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: CONCLUSIONS: Light to moderate alcohol consumption is associated with a reduced risk of multiple cardiovascular outcomes.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Associations of Alcohol Consumption with All-Cause and Cancer Mortalities in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Nationwide Population Cohort Study
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Cox proportional hazard regression analyses were used to calculate adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) with adjustments for age, sex, body mass index, smoking, exercise, comorbidities, diabetes duration, and medications.

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Associations of Alcohol Consumption with All-Cause and Cancer Mortalities in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Nationwide Population Cohort Study
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: Compared to non-drinkers, mild alcohol consumption was associated with reduced all-cause mortality (aHR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.80 to 0.82) and cancer mortality (aHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.86 to 0.89), while heavy drinking increased both all-cause (aHR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.07) and cancer mortalities (aHR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.11).

evidence_ledger.paper_title: Associations of Alcohol Consumption with All-Cause and Cancer Mortalities in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Nationwide Population Cohort Study
evidence_ledger.exact_source_passage: RESULTS: Among 2,642,359 participants (median follow-up, 7.8 years), 57.2%, 32.7%, and 10.1% were non, mild, and heavy drinkers, respectively.

suite.name: Intermittent Fasting vs Continuous Restriction
suite.query: Does intermittent fasting produce greater long-term weight loss than continuous calorie restriction when energy intake is comparable?
suite.focus: Isocaloric comparison alignment, adherence, context-dependent vs contradiction
